page: Microsoft Azure M128 is a memory-optimized virtual machine engineered for enterprise workloads requiring extensive system memory and substantial parallel compute capacity. Hosted on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor, the instance runs on 64 dedicated physical cores of the Intel Xeon 8280M processor with two threads per core, yielding 128 vCPUs operating at a base frequency of 2.7 GHz. Cache configuration includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 38 MB of shared L3 cache, backed by instruction support for AVX, AVX-512F, and AES. The server integrates 2048.0 GB of system memory, providing 16.0 GB of RAM per vCPU, alongside 15393 GB of bundled local SSD storage.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong parallel compute and memory streaming capabilities, counterbalanced by modest single-threaded throughput. In multi-threaded execution, the instance achieves an 87500.32 score in stress-ng multi-core testing, a PassMark CPU score of 53239.55, and 353.23 GB/sec in multi-threaded bzip3 decompression. The memory subsystem delivers uncached read throughput of 426.47 GB/sec and write bandwidth of 161.78 GB/sec. Application benchmarks reflect strong throughput with 80.9 million operations per second on Redis SET tasks and 56.82 GB/sec in static web serving. Conversely, single-core metrics fall into the lower performance tiers, shown by a stress-ng single-core score of 1038.39 and a Geekbench single-core result of 914.0.

Cost efficiency is centered around memory and I/O density. By pairing 2 TB of volatile memory with over 15 TB of high-speed local solid-state storage on a single virtualized host, the M128 provides strong consolidation efficiency for architectures that cannot be distributed across smaller nodes. However, workloads constrained by per-core clock speed or single-thread execution latency present poor resource efficiency on this tier.

The Microsoft Azure M128 is suited for large-scale in-memory databases like SAP HANA or Redis clusters, big data processing engines, enterprise resource planning backends, and memory-intensive data warehousing jobs. It is not intended for GPU-accelerated computing or tasks bound by single-core frequency.
